picked: Apache Kafka 4.3 (KRaft mode, three dedicated controllers), Apache License 2.0
why: 225 cars bursting over intermittent cellular links need a buffered backbone that decouples onboard store-and-forward from the fault engine and the dashboard, and Kafka 4.3 KRaft is the self-managed production pattern the customer owns outright.

choice: Tool: time series and telemetry storage
picked: InfluxDB 3 Core, dual licensed MIT OR Apache 2.0 at the user's choosing
why: 64 channels on 225 cars for 13 months of tabular and graphical history (C8, intake A3) is a telemetry-store workload first, and InfluxDB 3 Core is the permissive, self-hosted default the customer owns; TimescaleDB was weighed and set aside because its compression and continuous-aggregate features sit behind the non-OSI Timescale License.

choice: Tool: on site language model serving
why: The agent work surface model is self-hosted on the contractor's US cloud so the operator owns the weights, and vLLM 0.29.0 serves the 675B FP8 checkpoint with paged attention and continuous batching behind an OpenAI-compatible API; the version is pinned and change-boarded because the release cadence moves memory behaviour between minor versions.

choice: Tool: time synchronisation across sensors and systems
picked: chrony 4.9 with linuxptp 4.x where sub-second ordering is required, GPL-2.0
why: Slippery-rail hotspot logic joins slip/slide events across all trains by location and time (§3.4), so unsynchronised module clocks would produce confident wrong orderings; GNSS time from the Digi router disciplines onboard clocks and NTP/PTP discipline the cloud tier.

choice: Tool: observability of the running system
picked: Prometheus with Grafana and Loki, Prometheus Apache-2.0; Grafana and Loki AGPL-3.0 (run unmodified for internal use)
why: A monitoring system must itself be monitored: message delivery per car, queue depth behind cellular gaps, module heartbeats and alert delivery latency are the metrics whose silence is the first sign the fleet has gone blind.

choice: Tool: identity and access on site
why: A4 commits standalone user accounts with role-based access and MFA over an internet-facing view with unlimited user-specific licences, and Keycloak provides exactly that — OIDC login for the desk, yard and agent surfaces with roles mapped to mechanical-desk, yard, engineer and administrator.
